name: Evagrius Ponticus
knownFor: A deacon of Constantinople who became a monk of the Egyptian desert, and wrote of the eight tempting thoughts and of prayer.
dates: About 345 to 399 or 400. Palladius says he died at fifty-four. Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Gennadius gives 345 to 399; W. K. Lowther Clarke's note to Palladius puts the death in 399 or 400.
place: Ibora in Pontus; Constantinople; Nitria and Cellia in Egypt
role: Monk and writer on the ascetic life

keyWorks.title: Praktikos
keyWorks.about: a hundred short chapters on the ascetic life, the eight tempting thoughts and freedom from passion (held in Luke Dysinger's English)

keyWorks.title: Antirrhetikos
keyWorks.about: verses of Scripture set against each tempting thought, in eight parts, as Socrates describes it; Gennadius of Marseilles put it into Latin; not held

keyWorks.title: The Gnostic
keyWorks.about: fifty chapters for the learned, which Socrates quotes; not held

traces: Gennadius of Marseilles says he was the first, "or among the first at least", to teach the eight principal sins, and translated his work against them into Latin.
Palladius of Helenopolis, author of the Lausiac History, was his disciple, as Socrates of Constantinople says.
The Philokalia, the Greek collection on prayer compiled by Macarius of Corinth and Nikodemos the Hagiorite, lists works of his in its contents under the name of Evagrius the Monk.
remembered: Socrates of Constantinople copied passages from his books and wrote, "Whoever shall read these productions will be convinced of their excellence."
Jerome of Strido, writing in 415 against Pelagius, ranked him with the heretics and said his teaching on freedom from passion makes the mind "either a stone or a God."
Evagrius Scholasticus, writing in the sixth century, reports that the emperor Justinian condemned Origen, Didymus and Evagrius.

uncertain: His life is known mainly from his disciple Palladius, who writes in praise of him and tells it as he heard it from Evagrius himself.
The route from Constantinople differs. Palladius and Sozomen take him to Jerusalem first. Socrates of Constantinople says he went with Gregory of Nazianzus into Egypt.
Sozomen says the woman's husband plotted his death. Palladius says only that Evagrius imagined her husband had acted.

W. K. Lowther Clarke, who translated Palladius, notes that most of his works survive only in fragments in Greek and Latin, "having been suppressed for their Origenistic tendency," and that the chapter on him is missing from some copies of Palladius.

Evagrius Scholasticus names an "Evagrius" with Origen and Didymus in a dispute over Origen's teaching. He does not say which Evagrius. That it is this one is a reading of the passage, not his statement.
